title: Diagnosing pre-analytical variation
text:
SomaScan is a high-throughput aptamer-based proteomics platform capable of measuring thousands of proteins simultaneously (Candia 2025). Like other blood-based proteomic assays, SomaScan measurements can be sensitive to pre-analytical variation introduced during sample collection, processing, handling, and storage (Tatsumi et al. 2026; Candia et al. 2025). When such variation is systematic — affecting a subset of samples differently — it can produce spurious clusters in the data that are unrelated to the biological question of interest.
This resource documents a set of diagnostic and remediation strategies for identifying and handling pre-analytical variation in SomaScan data. The methods are illustrated with examples from a multi-site asthma proteomics study, but the approach generalises to any SomaScan dataset where sample quality or processing history is a concern.
The SomaLogic-provided lists of processing-sensitive proteins (fed-fasted state, freeze-thaw cycles, time to spin, time to decant, time to freeze) are central to these methods. These lists are not redistributed here; they can be obtained directly from SomaLogic. See the data/README.md file for instructions on where to place them once obtained.
The examples in this resource use plasma SomaScan data from a multi-site asthma proteomics study. The samples came from several collection sites, and the unexplained split that motivated this workflow was most visible within the Denver samples. I use Denver as the main worked example because that is where the clustering problem was clearest. The methods themselves are not specific to Denver; the same diagnostic and scoring steps can be applied to other SomaScan datasets where sample handling or fasting status may have introduced systematic structure.

title: Diagnosing pre-analytical variation
section: 2 Diagnosing the Cause of Unexplained Sample Clusters
text:
2 Diagnosing the Cause of Unexplained Sample Clusters

2.1 Motivation
After standard pre-processing and quality control, SomaScan data are often subjected to dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) and unsupervised clustering (e.g., k-means) to assess overall sample structure. In some datasets, two or more clusters emerge that cannot be attributed to the primary experimental variable (disease status, treatment arm, etc.) or to known technical factors such as assay batch or collection site.
When this occurs, a natural question is: could a pre-analytical processing difference — such as whether samples were collected from fasted or fed subjects, or experienced different freeze-thaw histories — be responsible?


2.2 Diagnostic Approach
SomaLogic provides, upon request, lists of proteins whose abundances are known to change substantially under specific pre-analytical conditions. For each condition, the list contains proteins along with their log2 fold change relative to a reference condition (e.g., protein abundance after 12 hours of fasting relative to the fed baseline).
The diagnostic approach works as follows:

Quantify the between-group signal. For each protein, fit a linear regression of log2 RFU on a categorical comparison variable, adjusting for relevant covariates (age, sex, disease status, ancestry PCs, assay batch). In the simplest case this is a binary contrast, but the grouping variable does not have to come from clustering. It can represent clusters, site, plate, processing group, or another experimental condition. The resulting beta coefficient for the selected contrast captures the direction and magnitude of each protein’s difference between the two groups being compared.
Compare to the processing-sensitive protein lists. For each processing condition, plot the known processing-induced log2 fold change (x-axis) against the observed between-group beta coefficient (y-axis).
Interpret the concordance. If a processing condition explains the separation between the two groups, its sensitive proteins should fall predominantly in quadrants I (both positive) and III (both negative) of this plot — meaning proteins that go up under that processing condition are also more abundant in one group, and proteins that go down are less abundant in that same group. A pattern scattered across all four quadrants indicates that condition is not the driver.



2.3 Example
The figure below shows this diagnostic applied to a subset of samples that formed two clusters unexplained by experimental variables. Each panel corresponds to one processing condition. The x-axis shows the known processing-induced log2 fold change provided by SomaLogic; the y-axis shows the observed cluster beta from the linear regression. Point size and colour encode statistical significance (−log₁₀ adjusted p-value). To focus on the most sensitive markers, each panel shows the five proteins with the largest positive processing effect and the five proteins with the largest negative processing effect, ranked by the x-axis fold-change column.


Code
# ── Data requirement ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# 01_cluster_diagnosis.r needs either:
#   (a) a pre-computed cache at data/de_cluster_results.rds  (fast path), OR
#   (b) an object called `adata_meta` already in the R environment.
#
# `adata_meta` must be a log2-transformed SomaScan ADAT joined with sample
# metadata, filtered to biological samples, and augmented with a 'Cluster'
# column ('Big' / 'Small') from a prior k-means step.
#
# To use the fast path, run 01_cluster_diagnosis.r once interactively with
# adata_meta loaded; it will write data/de_cluster_results.rds automatically.
# Subsequent renders (including this page) will read that cache instead.
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

library(here)
source(here::here("scripts/01_cluster_diagnosis.r"))
print(diag_figure)








Figure 1: Diagnostic comparison of processing-sensitive protein fold changes (x-axis, from SomaLogic) versus observed between-cluster beta coefficients (y-axis). Each panel shows the five most positive and five most negative processing-sensitive proteins ranked by the SomaLogic x-axis fold-change column. Concordance in quadrants I and III implicates that condition as the likely driver of the sample clustering. In this example, only the Fed-Fasted State panel shows clear concordance, indicating that fasting status drove the observed clusters.







2.4 Interpreting the Results
In the example above, only the Fed-Fasted State panel shows clear concordance: proteins known to increase after fasting (positive Time_12_hours fold change) were consistently more abundant in one cluster, and proteins known to decrease after fasting were consistently less abundant in that cluster. No such pattern was observed for freeze-thaw cycles, time to spin, time to decant, or time to freeze.
This pattern strongly suggests that a subset of samples were collected from subjects in a fasted state, while the remainder were collected from fed subjects, and that this biological/pre-analytical difference — rather than disease status or technical batch effects — is responsible for the clustering.


2.5 Data Requirements
To run this diagnostic in your own dataset you need:

Log2-transformed SomaScan data with a categorical comparison variable. A cluster label (Big / Small) is one example, but clustering is not a prerequisite. The same diagnostic can be used to compare site, plate, processing group, or another experimental condition. For the plotted diagnostic, the comparison should be a defined binary contrast or a selected coefficient from a multi-level categorical variable.
SomaLogic processing-sensitive protein lists (CSV format, one file per condition). These are available from SomaLogic upon request and should be placed in the data/ directory of this repository. They are excluded from version control; see data/README.md.
Sample metadata including any covariates to be included in the linear model (e.g., age, sex, disease status, ancestry PCs, assay batch).

The annotated R script implementing this diagnostic is available at scripts/01_cluster_diagnosis.r.

title: Diagnosing pre-analytical variation
text:
3 Fed-Fasted Score Calculation

3.1 Motivation
The diagnostic plot above tells us which processing condition best matches the unexplained sample clustering. In this example, the Fed-Fasted State panel showed the clearest concordance: proteins known to increase after fasting were also higher in one of the sample clusters, and proteins known to decrease after fasting were lower in that same cluster.
After seeing that pattern, the next useful step is to turn the protein-level signal into a sample-level score. The goal of the score is simple: for each sample, estimate how strongly its protein profile looks like the fasted pattern described by the SomaLogic fed-fasted experiment. This is consistent with SOMAScan work showing that nutrient state can shift serum protein profiles (Han et al. 2021).


3.2 Score Definition
For both scoring strategies below, I use the same weighted score. Let R_sp be the log2 RFU for sample s and protein p, let mean(R_p) be the mean log2 RFU for protein p across samples, and let beta_p be the SomaLogic fed-fasted effect size from Time_12_hours.
The score for sample s is:
\[
S_s = \sum_{p \in P} (R_{sp} - \bar{R}_p) \times \beta_p
\]
Here, P is the selected set of fed-fasted sensitive proteins. Centering each protein first makes the score depend on whether a sample is high or low for that protein relative to the dataset. Multiplying by Time_12_hours preserves the direction of the fasting effect. A protein that increases after fasting gets a positive weight, while a protein that decreases after fasting gets a negative weight. In this way, both types of proteins contribute in the same biological direction to the final score.


3.3 Strategy 1: Effect-Size Thresholding
The first strategy is to keep fed-fasted proteins with stronger SomaLogic effect sizes. Starting from the full fed-fasted CSV, we keep proteins with a non-missing Time_12_hours value and then apply a threshold to the absolute log2 fold change:
\[
|\beta_p| \geq c
\]
where c is the chosen effect-size cutoff. In this example, I scanned several cutoffs based on the distribution of abs(Time_12_hours) and compared the resulting score to the major PCA axis that captured the unexplained sample split. The score remained strong when proteins with abs(Time_12_hours) >= 0.25 were used, while weaker-effect proteins were more likely to add noise. For that reason, 0.25 is a practical default for this example, not a universal rule.
This thresholding strategy is easy to understand and easy to reproduce. It asks only one question: which proteins have a large enough known fed-fasted effect that they should be trusted in the score?


3.4 Strategy 2: Independent Protein Selection
The second strategy tries to avoid giving too much influence to groups of highly correlated proteins. This is similar in spirit to clumping in PLINK. In polygenic risk score analysis, clumping keeps the strongest genetic variant in a correlated group and removes nearby variants that are in high linkage disequilibrium. The aim is to keep the strongest signal without counting the same correlated information many times (Chang et al. 2015).
Here the objects are proteins rather than genetic variants, so there is no genomic window. Instead, I rank proteins by the absolute log2 fold change in the SomaLogic Time_12_hours column. At each step, the protein with the largest remaining abs(Time_12_hours) value is kept, and proteins that are highly correlated with that selected protein are removed. The algorithm is:

Start with fed-fasted proteins with non-missing Time_12_hours.
From the proteins still available, select the one with the largest absolute Time_12_hours log2 fold change (abs(Time_12_hours)).
Remove any other available proteins that are too strongly correlated with the selected protein, using the chosen correlation threshold.
Repeat until no proteins remain.
Calculate the same weighted score using only the retained proteins.

I call the result an independent protein score. The word “independent” is practical rather than absolute: the retained proteins are not guaranteed to be statistically independent, but they are less redundant under the chosen correlation threshold.
In this example, the correlation matrix used for clumping is estimated from all sites except Denver. That choice matters. Denver is the site where the fed-fasted-like split was most visible, so including Denver when estimating protein-protein correlations can make proteins look correlated because of the very artifact we are trying to measure. Using the non-Denver samples gives a cleaner reference for deciding which proteins are redundant. In other settings, the same correlation structure could also be estimated from publicly available healthy-control SomaScan data, if the assay version and protein annotations are compatible with the study being analyzed.
Several correlation thresholds can be tried, such as 0.60, 0.75, 0.80, and 0.90. A lower threshold gives a smaller and less redundant protein set; a higher threshold keeps more proteins and behaves more like the full fed-fasted list. In the original analysis, correlation calculated without Denver gave better separation of the suspected fed-fasted groups, especially around the 0.75 threshold.


3.5 Correlation Diagnostics
Before using the score, I like to look at the correlation structure of the selected proteins. The first plot shows the proteins retained by the simple abs(Time_12_hours) >= 0.25 rule. The independent-protein tabs show the clumping-like selection at several correlation thresholds. In all plots, the upper triangle uses correlations calculated from all samples, while the lower triangle uses correlations calculated after excluding Denver.

Log2 FC > 0.25Independent: cor < 0.60Independent: cor < 0.75Independent: cor < 0.95










Figure 2: Correlation among fed-fasted proteins selected by absolute SomaLogic Time_12_hours log2 fold-change threshold of 0.25. The upper triangle uses all samples and the lower triangle excludes Denver. Red labels indicate proteins higher after fasting; blue labels indicate proteins lower after fasting.















Figure 3: Color-coded correlation plot for independent fed-fasted protein selection using correlation threshold 0.60. The upper triangle uses all samples and the lower triangle excludes Denver. Red labels indicate proteins selected only when Denver is excluded, blue labels indicate proteins selected only when all samples are used, and purple labels indicate proteins selected in both cases.















Figure 4: Color-coded correlation plot for independent fed-fasted protein selection using correlation threshold 0.75. The upper triangle uses all samples and the lower triangle excludes Denver. Red labels indicate proteins selected only when Denver is excluded, blue labels indicate proteins selected only when all samples are used, and purple labels indicate proteins selected in both cases.















Figure 5: Color-coded correlation plot for independent fed-fasted protein selection using correlation threshold 0.95. The upper triangle uses all samples and the lower triangle excludes Denver. Red labels indicate proteins selected only when Denver is excluded, blue labels indicate proteins selected only when all samples are used, and purple labels indicate proteins selected in both cases.










3.6 Using The Score
Once the score is calculated, I use it as a QC summary of the fed-fasted signal. A two-component Gaussian mixture model can be fit to the score to identify samples with higher fasted-like signal versus lower fasted-like signal (Benaglia et al. 2009). Those labels can then be compared to PCA clusters, collection site, and other metadata.
The plots below show the GMM fit for each score. The histogram shows the score distribution, the black curves show the two fitted mixture components, and the colored density curves show how the existing k-means clusters are distributed along the score. The small table inside each plot summarizes how many samples from each k-means cluster fall into the lower-score and higher-score GMM groups.

Log2 FC > 0.25Independent: cor < 0.60Independent: cor < 0.75Independent: cor < 0.95










Figure 6: Gaussian mixture model fit of the fed-fasted score calculated using proteins with absolute SomaLogic Time_12_hours log2 fold change greater than or equal to 0.25.















Figure 7: Gaussian mixture model fit of the fed-fasted score calculated using independent proteins selected with correlation threshold 0.60. Protein correlations used for selection were calculated after excluding Denver.















Figure 8: Gaussian mixture model fit of the fed-fasted score calculated using independent proteins selected with correlation threshold 0.75. Protein correlations used for selection were calculated after excluding Denver.















Figure 9: Gaussian mixture model fit of the fed-fasted score calculated using independent proteins selected with correlation threshold 0.95. Protein correlations used for selection were calculated after excluding Denver.










3.7 Sample Filtering vs. Covariate Adjustment
After identifying samples with high fed-fasted score, there are two practical ways to use this information in the downstream analysis.
The first option is sample filtering. In this approach, samples assigned to the higher fed-fasted-score GMM group are removed before differential expression analysis. This is useful when the score identifies a distinct subset of samples that appears to be affected by a pre-analytical difference rather than by the main biological question. The advantage is that we are not asking the statistical model to repair a strong handling artifact after the fact. The tradeoff is that we lose samples, and this can reduce power or change the analysis population if the removed samples are not evenly distributed across phenotypes, sites, or other study variables.
The second option is covariate adjustment. In this approach, all samples are kept, and the fed-fasted score, or sometimes the GMM class based on the score, is included as a covariate in the model. This can be attractive when the total sample size is limited, when the score varies continuously rather than forming a clear outlier group, or when filtering would remove too many samples from an important subgroup. The tradeoff is that adjustment assumes the score captures the processing effect in a way the model can handle. If the affected samples form a strong separate cluster, or if the processing signal is highly heterogeneous, a single covariate may not fully remove the artifact.
So I do not think there is one universal choice. The decision depends on the experiment, the total number of samples, how much heterogeneity is present, and how strongly the score is tangled with the biology we want to test. In this example, the score and the PCA/k-means structure pointed to a smaller group of samples with a clear fed-fasted-like signal. We found that filtering was the better option for this dataset, so the smaller high-score group was filtered out before the downstream differential expression analysis.

title: Diagnosing pre-analytical variation
text:
4 Differential Expression After Fed-Fasted Filtering
After filtering the smaller high-score group, the next question is how to run the differential expression analysis. The data here are already normalized SomaScan RFU values on the log2 scale, so we can use linear modeling methods directly on the protein abundance matrix.
This is where limma is still a reasonable baseline model (Ritchie et al. 2015). We are not using voom here because voom was designed mainly for RNA-seq-style count data, where the mean-variance relationship is tied to count sampling and negative binomial-like behavior (Law et al. 2014). SomaScan RFU values are not read counts. After the SomaScan normalization steps and log2 transformation, the working data are continuous protein abundance measurements, so the ordinary limma linear model with empirical Bayes variance moderation is appropriate as a fixed-effect baseline.
However, this study includes samples from multiple sites. We saw earlier that site contributed a large amount of structure to the proteomic data. A fixed effect model can include site as a covariate, but that is not always the best way to represent site-to-site heterogeneity, especially when the sites are better thought of as sampled study centers with their own background shifts. For that reason, we also tested random-effect models where site is included as a random intercept.
The cleaned model helpers are in scripts/03_de_analysis.r. That script was organized from the older development scripts and contains:

fit_limma_model() for the fixed-effect limma analysis without voom.
fit_dream_model() for the mixed-effect Dream analysis with site as a random effect.
fit_lmer_test_model() for a per-protein lmerTest comparison model.
fit_lmer_seq_model() as an optional placeholder for an lmerSeq comparison model.
run_dream_all_samples() and run_dream_indep075_filter() for the worked comparison used below.
volcano_break_axis(), plot_all_samples_dream_volcano(), and plot_indep075_dream_volcano() for the volcano plots.

The important pattern from testing these approaches was that modeling site as a random effect improved the signal compared with the fixed-effect limma baseline. Among the random-effect approaches, Dream was the most useful for this workflow because it combines linear mixed models with limma-style empirical Bayes moderation (Hoffman and Roussos 2021).
We also used split eBayes in the Dream framework. SomaScan proteins are measured in different dilution groups, and the technical variance structure is not necessarily the same across those groups. Applying empirical Bayes moderation separately within each dilution group lets the variance borrowing happen within a more comparable set of measurements. In our analysis, this split eBayes Dream model was more powerful than the alternatives we tested.
The volcano plots below show the focused comparison used in this repo. The first plot uses all samples. The second plot uses the same Dream split-eBayes model after filtering samples by the independent fed-fasted score at correlation threshold 0.75. This keeps the model fixed and lets us see the effect of removing the smaller high-score group.
The point of the all-sample plot is not that it produces many significant proteins. It is the baseline comparison showing that, before filtering, the asthma differential-expression signal is relatively muted. Using the same display threshold shown in the volcano plots, 23 proteins are highlighted in the all-sample model, compared with 70 proteins after fed-fasted filtering. After filtering, many more biologically meaningful proteins become visible, which is why sample filtering was useful in this dataset.
IgE is an outlying signal in both dimensions: it has a very large log2 fold change on the x-axis and a very large -log10 adjusted p-value on the y-axis. In a usual single-scale volcano plot, this stretches the axes so much that the remaining proteins are compressed into a small part of the figure. For that reason, we used a customized volcano plot with broken/faceted axes so that the IgE result remains visible while the rest of the differential-expression pattern can still be inspected.

After Fed-Fasted FilteringAll Samples










Figure 10: Volcano plot for Active Asthma differential expression after filtering the higher-score GMM group identified from the independent fed-fasted score at correlation threshold 0.75. The model is Dream with site as a random effect and split empirical Bayes moderation by SomaScan dilution group. After filtering, more highlighted and biologically interpretable proteins become visible. Customized axis breaks are used because the IgE log2 fold change and adjusted significance are much larger than the rest of the proteins.















Figure 11: Volcano plot for Active Asthma differential expression using all samples. The model is Dream with site as a random effect and split empirical Bayes moderation by SomaScan dilution group. This panel is included as the baseline comparison before fed-fasted filtering; the broader asthma signal is relatively muted when all samples are retained. Customized axis breaks are used because the IgE log2 fold change and adjusted significance are much larger than the rest of the proteins.

title: Better design before analysis. Better evidence after it.
text:
PRACTICAL SOMASCAN GUIDANCE



SomaSens is a growing collection of practical notes for designing SomaScan studies, recognizing unwanted variation, and making defensible analysis decisions.
Explore pre-analytical variation Plan plate randomization

title: Better design before analysis. Better evidence after it.
text:
Why this matters
SomaScan measurements can be sensitive to what happens before the assay, including fed-versus-fasted state, freeze-thaw history, hemolysis, and delays between collection, processing, and freezing (Han et al. 2021; Candia et al. 2025; Tatsumi et al. 2026). If these factors differ systematically between study groups, they can create broad protein shifts, unexplained sample clusters, or misleading associations.
Known processing-sensitive protein signatures can sometimes help diagnose the source of a problem. The current detailed report shows how to compare an observed between-group signal with those signatures and how to calculate a sample-level fed-fasted score.

The practical conclusion
Diagnosis does not guarantee that the affected measurements can be repaired. When a processing effect is large, excluding a clearly defined set of affected samples may be more defensible than relying on statistical adjustment alone, although filtering also reduces power and can introduce selection bias. The best protection is consistent sample preparation, balanced study design, and a complete record of what happened to every sample.

title: Better design before analysis. Better evidence after it.
text:
Guidance in this site


Diagnose processing variation
Use known processing-sensitive proteins to investigate unexpected sample structure, calculate a fed-fasted score, and evaluate filtering decisions.
Read the detailed report →


Randomize samples over plates
See good and bad allocation patterns and learn why assay QC and normalization cannot rescue a design in which biology is confounded with plate or well position.
View the design guide →


Filter SOMAmers for CSF
A future guide will document matrix-aware criteria for choosing SOMAmers in cerebrospinal fluid analyses, with transparent reasons for every exclusion.
See the planned scope →

title: Better design before analysis. Better evidence after it.
text:
A simple working principle


1
Prevent
Standardize collection and processing wherever possible.


2
Record
Keep sample-level times, handling events, storage history, plate, and well.


3
Balance
Distribute biological groups across plates and available well positions.


4
Diagnose
Inspect structure before testing the primary biological hypothesis.

title: Randomizing samples over plates
text:
SomaScan uses internal controls, calibration, quality-control samples, and several normalization steps to reduce known sources of assay variation (SomaLogic, Inc. 2021; Candia et al. 2022). Those procedures are important, but they do not make experimental design irrelevant. Residual or unanticipated technical variation can remain, and no downstream adjustment can separate two effects that are perfectly confounded.
If all cases are placed on one plate and all controls on another, for example, every case-control difference is also a plate difference. The data cannot tell which explanation is responsible. Balanced block randomization is intended to prevent this problem (Burger, Vaudel, and Barsnes 2021).

title: Randomizing samples over plates
section: Bad design: group and plate are confounded
text:
Bad design: group and plate are confounded
In this simplified example, Plate 1 contains only Group A and Plate 2 contains only Group B. A plate shift—regardless of its cause—will look exactly like a group effect.


  
    Plate 1
    
      AAAA
      AAAA
      AAAA
      AAAA
    
  
  
    Plate 2
    
      BBBB
      BBBB
      BBBB
      BBBB
    
  

 Group A Group B
Bad: study group is perfectly confounded with plate. Plate adjustment cannot recover an independently estimable group effect.

title: Randomizing samples over plates
section: Bad design: plate is balanced, position is not
text:
Bad design: plate is balanced, position is not
Putting both groups on every plate is necessary, but not always sufficient. Here, Group A always occupies the first two rows and Group B the last two rows. Any row, edge, timing, or pipetting-order effect can still align with the biological comparison.


  
    Plate 1
    
      AAAA
      AAAA
      BBBB
      BBBB
    
  
  
    Plate 2
    
      AAAA
      AAAA
      BBBB
      BBBB
    
  

 Group A Group B
Bad: each plate is numerically balanced, but group remains confounded with row and processing order.

title: Randomizing samples over plates
section: Better design: blocked, balanced, and randomized
text:
Better design: blocked, balanced, and randomized
In the better example, both groups appear in equal numbers on each plate and their positions change across plates. The exact map should be generated with a recorded random seed and constrained only enough to achieve balance on the important design variables. This distributes—not necessarily eliminates—any remaining technical variation.

title: Randomizing samples over plates
Randomizing samples over plates
text:
Recommended workflow

Define the model first. State the primary contrast and the covariates or blocking variables that the analysis will need.
Obtain the operational plate template. Mark the wells reserved for assay controls and identify the actual study-sample capacity.
Create representative blocks. Allocate each plate approximately the same proportions of the major study groups.
Randomize within constraints. Randomize study samples over the available wells while checking rows, columns, edges, and processing order.
Audit the proposed map. Cross-tabulate every important variable against plate and, where relevant, row and column.
Freeze and export the map. Save the random seed, script, final plate map, deviations from the plan, and the map actually run.
Retain technical variables. Include plate, well, run, and relevant QC outputs in the analysis-ready metadata.







TipA useful audit question



If one plate failed completely, would the primary biological comparison still exist in the remaining plates? If the answer is no, revisit the allocation.

title: Randomizing samples over plates
text:
Minimum metadata to retain
Keep, at minimum, a stable sample identifier, participant identifier, study group, collection site and time, processing timestamps, fasting state, freeze-thaw count, storage location, shipment, assay run, plate, row, column, and any departure from the planned workflow. Use explicit missing values rather than interpreting a blank as “no event.”
